name: 1Day Sooner: charityevals' estimate
beneficiaries_note: Our build: most of the result is pandemic risk, which is everyone's, so it is spread by world population; the malaria vaccine branch (sub-Saharan Africa) and hepatitis C (worldwide) are about 23% of it and left in the world figure.
summary: 1Day Sooner (Delaware, working mostly from the US, the UK and five African countries) represents volunteers for human challenge studies and campaigns for faster vaccines and pandemic preparedness. This model of all its 2024 work ($2.4M, its latest Form 990) comes to about 5 years of healthy life per $1,000, from about 0.4 to 75 on the combined range, so the result is mostly uncertainty: most of it is its pandemic work (an FDA preparedness programme, plans for challenge studies in a pandemic, indoor air cleaning) valued as a typical pandemic project's cut in the forecast risk, plus its part in stopping a California bill that would have banned far-UV air cleaners; its hepatitis C challenge-study work (valued by the 1.5 years it says it cut from the Toronto study) and its malaria vaccine campaign (by children vaccinated sooner, net of what the Gavi money would do elsewhere) add about 23%. Every branch is discounted for missing data, and the result moves most with the discount rate and a typical pandemic dollar's effect.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

Hepatitis C: share of the cost spent on hepatitis C challenge studies and vaccines
rows.explainer: The hepatitis C challenge programme (embedded in the Toronto University Health Network team: study design, materials, compensation, a Toronto advertising campaign, a chatbot, a forecasting competition, assay standardisation) and the hepatitis C vaccine campaign inside Warp Speed 2.0 (the Washington dinner, the December 2024 conference with Francis Collins). The Form 990 has one programme line, so the share is our judgment from the funding proposal, which describes five programme areas of which this is the flagship with the most staff work: 27% (15% to 40%), about $650,000 with overhead.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: years cut from the Toronto challenge study's timeline by the design changes 1Day proposed

source.title: 1Day Sooner, Funding Proposal 2025-2026 to Open Philanthropy (lightly redacted public version, shared on the EA Forum 2 July 2025)
source.page: Hepatitis C, Case Study: UHN Study Design Improvements
source.quote: As a result, as of July 2024, the proposed protocol will take about 1.5 fewer years to complete, all else being equal, without significantly increasing risk to participants.

rows.explainer: 1Day Sooner's own account: it proposed running steps in parallel (inocula for several genotypes at once) and earlier safety gates (four weeks after inoculation instead of a sustained response at week 12), which the study team approved. The charity's own count, not checked by anyone else; its trust is in hcv_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: share of the study time saved that brings a licensed vaccine forward
rows.explainer: A challenge study gives early efficacy data, but a vaccine still needs field trials, licensure and purchase; a year saved in one study moves the end only if the study is on the critical path, later steps don't absorb it and the same changes would not have come later anyway (1Day says the rest of the team made no substantial effort on speed, so it was the main driver). The 2024 proposal reports delayed start dates at both the Toronto and Oxford studies (hiring, contracting, a protocol Health Canada asked to resubmit). 0.4 (0.1 to 0.8), our judgment; it holds the would-have-come-anyway question too, so there is no separate counterfactual row.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: share of the design result due to 2024's spending
rows.explainer: 1Day worked with the Toronto team over two years ("integrated into the University Health Network hepatitis C CHIM team over the last two years", the 2025-2026 proposal), with the result counted as of July 2024; its staff and the 2024 focus groups and town halls behind the case for the changes fall mostly in 2024. Half (a third to 70%), our judgment, so the 2024 cost meets only its part of the result (Convention 11).

rows.label: Hepatitis C: years a vaccine comes sooner, credited to 2024's work
Hepatitis C: chance a vaccine this study helps is licensed and used
rows.explainer: Whether a hepatitis C vaccine is licensed and used at all, the one event the branch hangs on (drawn as all or nothing). No vaccine exists (WHO); the one candidate that reached an efficacy trial, a viral-vector prime-boost in people who inject drugs, failed to prevent chronic infection (Page et al., NEJM 2021). Vaccines entering clinical development are licensed roughly one time in ten; a challenge model makes screening candidates cheaper and faster, which is its point. 20% (5% to 50%), our judgment.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: new infections a year, worldwide

source.title: WHO, Hepatitis C fact sheet (28 July 2026)
source.quote: Globally, an estimated 47 million people have chronic hepatitis C virus infection, with about 0.9 million new infections occurring per year.

rows.explainer: WHO's latest estimate (2024 data).

rows.label: Hepatitis C: deaths a year, worldwide

source.title: WHO, Hepatitis C fact sheet (28 July 2026)
source.quote: In 2024, approximately 239 000 people died from hepatitis C, mostly from cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (primary liver cancer).

rows.explainer: WHO's latest estimate. Over new infections it gives the deaths a year of infections cause in today's steady state, about 0.27 per infection; the next row allows for more cures by the time a vaccine arrives.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: share of today's deaths per infection still expected when a vaccine is in use
rows.explainer: Direct-acting antivirals cure over 95% of those treated, but by the end of 2024 only 36% of people with chronic infection knew it and about 20% had been treated (WHO fact sheet). By the late 2030s, when a vaccine could be in use, more infections will be found and cured before they kill; GBD forecasts still have hepatitis C's burden falling slowly. 40% (15% to 80%) of today's deaths per infection, our judgment.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: deaths averted per infection averted, once a vaccine is in use
Hepatitis C: share of the world's new infections a vaccine in use averts
rows.explainer: Coverage of those at risk (people who inject drugs, unsafe medical injections in a few countries) times efficacy, which for a first vaccine may be partial. 15% (5% to 40%), about 135,000 infections a year, our judgment. Cross-check: the study 1Day commissioned put a 5-year acceleration at 185,000 to 830,000 fewer infections (37,000 to 166,000 a year; the proposal's note 1), around this figure.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: years from 2024 until a vaccine would be in use
rows.explainer: The challenge studies had not started by mid-2024; then candidate testing, field efficacy trials, licensure and purchase. 12 years (8 to 20), our judgment; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: years from an infection to the death it causes
rows.explainer: Chronic infection leads to cirrhosis in 15% to 30% within 20 years (WHO fact sheet), and deaths come from cirrhosis and liver cancer after that: 25 years (15 to 35), our judgment; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Hepatitis C: discount for the wait until the deaths averted
Hepatitis C: deaths averted (expected, discounted, before adjustments)
rows.formula: hcv_years_forward * hcv_p_vaccine * hcv_new_infections * hcv_vaccine_share_averted * hcv_deaths_per_infection * hcv_wait

rows.label: Hepatitis C: illness averted, as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: Illness as a share of the deaths' value: years lived with disability over years of life lost in hepatitis C's burden (WHO GHE 2023, world: 2.3% of its DALYs are illness), about 2.4%.

Malaria vaccines: share of the cost spent on malaria vaccine deployment
rows.explainer: The malaria vaccine campaign for faster R21 and RTS,S rollout: part-time staff in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Kenya, Tanzania and Zambia, a communications consultant, polling, a white paper, op-eds and a congressional letter, and the $11,450 of grants to sub-Saharan Africa. One programme line in the 990, so our judgment from the funding proposal's account of 2024: 26% (15% to 40%), about $630,000 with overhead.

rows.label: Malaria vaccines: children a year fully vaccinated sooner or added because of all advocacy for faster rollout in 2024
rows.explainer: What every group pushing for faster rollout in 2024 (PATH, the Malaria No More and RBM networks, African health ministries and leaders, 1Day Sooner) adds to the children vaccinated each year while the faster rollout lasts, beyond what Gavi and the countries would have done anyway (so the field's counterfactual is in this row). Gavi's 2026-2030 plan targets 50 million children (10 million a year), higher than 1Day expected, with no sign it was moved by the campaign; the Serum Institute can make 100 million doses a year against plans under 250 million by 2030. 167,000 a year (33,000 to 833,000), our judgment: about 1.7% of Gavi's yearly target; counted for the shared years a win counts ($win_years_counted).

rows.label: Malaria vaccines: deaths averted per child fully vaccinated (four doses)

source.title: Schmit et al., The public health impact and cost-effectiveness of the R21/Matrix-M malaria vaccine, Lancet Infectious Diseases 2024;24:465-475 (doi:10.1016/S1473-3099(23)00816-2), as summarised by the Immunization Economics community
source.quote: 632 [range 268 to 633] malaria deaths for every 100,000 fully vaccinated children in perennial settings

rows.explainer: Imperial College's model of R21 across sub-Saharan Africa over 15 years: 632 deaths averted per 100,000 fully vaccinated children in perennial settings, 663 (216 to 719) in seasonal ones; the range spans both. 1Day's own figure, about 1,500 lives per million doses, is the same at four doses a child.

rows.explainer: How far 1Day's pandemic outputs beat or trail a typical pandemic project. In its favour: the FDA Emerging Pathogens Preparedness Program it designed was in the FDA's FY24 legislative proposals, a bipartisan bill and the Senate draft of the Pandemic All-Hazards Preparedness Act, with report language in both appropriations bills; its challenge-study ethics recommendations went into the 100 Days Mission's implementation roadmap; a UK parliamentary inquiry drew on its evidence. Against: the FDA programme got no money and dropped out of the FY25 proposals, and the pathogen biobank and containment-bed agreement were still proposals. 0.8 (0.4 to 1.2), our judgment, near the Johns Hopkins Center (0.73) and Blueprint (0.75).

rows.explainer: Good not counted above, as a share of the modelled value: far-UV and other air cleaning against everyday respiratory infections if the Safe Air Research Alliance and the California market lead to installations (about 4%); an FDA preparedness programme also speeding peacetime vaccines (about 2%); hepatitis C treatment costs averted and the branch's other outputs (the chatbot, forecasts, assay standards) (about 2%); malaria's later-life income gains and fewer clinical cases treated (about 2%). 10% (2% to 30%), our judgment; peers 5% to 15%.

rows.label: Harm: risk to challenge-study volunteers it recruits or promotes, as a share of modelled value

rows.label: Harm: friction with the bodies it criticises, as a share of modelled value
